$$V_\ell\,\Delta P = RT\ln\frac{P}{P^*}$$

Solve for $\ln(P/P^*)$:

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{V_\ell\,\Delta P}{RT}$$

Convert $\Delta P$ to pascals:
$$\Delta P = 50\,\text{atm} \times 1.013\times10^5\,\text{Pa/atm} = 5.065\times10^6\,\text{Pa}$$

Compute the numerator:
$$V_\ell\,\Delta P = 1.689\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol} \times 5.065\times10^6\,\text{Pa} = 85.55\,\text{J/mol}$$

Compute the denominator:
$$RT = 8.314 \times 2200 = 18{,}291\,\text{J/mol}$$

Therefore:
$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{85.55}{18{,}291} = 4.677\times10^{-3}$$

$$\frac{P}{P^*} = e^{4.677\times10^{-3}} \approx 1.00469$$

$$P = 1.00469 \times 0.4572\,\text{atm} = 0.4593\,\text{atm}$$

**Result:** $P \approx 0.4593\,\text{atm}$ under 50 atm of applied mechanical pressure.

---

### Part (d) — Fractional increase and physical interpretation

$$\frac{P - P^*}{P^*} = \frac{0.4593 - 0.4572}{0.4572} = \frac{0.00215}{0.4572} \approx 4.7\times10^{-3} = \mathbf{0.47\%}$$

Alternatively, directly from $\ln(P/P^*) = 4.677\times10^{-3}$, the fractional increase is $\approx 0.47\%$.

**Comment:** Even applying 50 atm of extra mechanical pressure raises the vapour pressure of liquid indium by less than **0.5%** at 2200 K. This is a general feature of condensed phases: because $V_\ell$ is small ($\sim 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}$) relative to the gas-phase molar volume ($V_g = RT/P \sim 1.5\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}$ here), the mechanical-compression effect on vapour pressure is negligible compared to the temperature effect captured by the Clausius–Clapeyron equation. Huge pressures would be required to produce a meaningful change — this is why temperature control, not mechanical pressure, is the primary lever for managing vapour pressure in metal processing furnaces.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $P^* \approx 0.457\,\text{atm}$ at 2200 K; (b) $V_\ell = 1.689\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}$; (c) $P \approx 0.4593\,\text{atm}$; (d) fractional increase $\approx 0.47\%$ — mechanical pressure has a negligible effect on vapour pressure of condensed metals.
common_mistakes: **Using the wrong reference state in Clausius–Clapeyron.** Students often treat 298 K as the reference and look for a vapour pressure there, rather than anchoring to the normal boiling point (where $P = 1\,\text{atm}$ by definition). The normal boiling point is the natural anchor because it directly satisfies the equilibrium condition $P_\text{vap} = P_\text{atm}$.

**Forgetting to convert $\Delta P$ to pascals before substituting into $V_\ell\,\Delta P = RT\ln(P/P^*)$.** Leaving $\Delta P$ in atm while $V_\ell$ is in m³/mol gives an answer in m³·atm/mol rather than joules, making the ratio $V_\ell\Delta P / RT$ dimensionally inconsistent. Always convert pressure to Pa so that $\text{m}^3 \times \text{Pa} = \text{J}$.

**Confusing the mechanical-pressure effect with the Clausius–Clapeyron temperature effect.** Some students try to use the Clausius–Clapeyron equation for part (c), adjusting temperature. The two effects are distinct: Clausius–Clapeyron relates vapour pressure to temperature along the liquid–gas phase boundary; the $V_\ell\Delta P$ relation describes how an extra inert mechanical load on the liquid surface shifts the chemical potential of the liquid phase and thus raises its equilibrium vapour pressure at fixed temperature.

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure Enhancement Over a Platinum Nanowire
L4|hard.statement:
Platinum nanowires are fabricated by electrodeposition and have cylindrical geometries with very small radii. A materials engineer needs to assess the thermodynamic stability of platinum vapour over the curved surface of a nanowire compared to a flat bulk platinum surface at $T = 1800\,\text{K}$.

The following data are given for platinum at $1800\,\text{K}$:
- Equilibrium vapour pressure over a flat (bulk) Pt surface: $P^* = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{atm}$
- Surface energy (surface tension) of Pt: $\gamma = 2.40\,\text{J/m}^2$
- Molar mass of Pt: $M = 195.08\,\text{g/mol}$
- Density of Pt: $\rho = 19{,}300\,\text{kg/m}^3$
- Gas constant: $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

For a cylindrical geometry, the Laplace pressure is $\Delta P = \gamma / r$ (only one principal radius of curvature contributes for an infinite cylinder, compared to $2\gamma/r$ for a sphere).

**(a)** Calculate the molar volume $\underline{V}_\text{Pt}$ of solid platinum.

**(b)** Using the Kelvin equation adapted for a cylinder, derive and compute the ratio $P/P^*$ for a platinum nanowire of radius $r = 5\,\text{nm}$.

**(c)** Hence determine the absolute vapour pressure $P$ over the nanowire surface at $1800\,\text{K}$.

**(d)** The engineer proposes to anneal two platinum nanowire samples simultaneously in the same sealed furnace at $1800\,\text{K}$: sample S1 has wire radius $r_1 = 5\,\text{nm}$ and sample S2 has wire radius $r_2 = 50\,\text{nm}$. Using the Kelvin equation, predict qualitatively and quantitatively what will happen to the two samples over time. Calculate $P/P^*$ for S2 and compare with S1.
L4|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Molar volume of solid Pt

The molar volume is:
$$\underline{V}_\text{Pt} = \frac{M}{\rho} = \frac{195.08 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg/mol}}{19{,}300\,\text{kg/m}^3}$$

$$\boxed{\underline{V}_\text{Pt} = 1.011 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}}$$

---

### Part (b) — Kelvin equation for a cylinder

The Kelvin equation is derived from equating the change in chemical potential of the condensed phase (due to the Laplace pressure) to the change in chemical potential of the vapour (ideal gas).

**Chemical potential increase of the solid** due to the Laplace pressure $\Delta P = \gamma/r$ pressing inward on the curved surface:
$$\Delta\mu_\text{solid} = \underline{V}_\text{Pt} \cdot \Delta P = \underline{V}_\text{Pt} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{r}$$

**Chemical potential change of the vapour** (ideal gas) from vapour pressure $P^*$ to $P$:
$$\Delta\mu_\text{vapour} = RT \ln\frac{P}{P^*}$$

**Equating** (equilibrium condition $\mu_\text{solid} = \mu_\text{vapour}$):
$$\underline{V}_\text{Pt} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{r} = RT \ln\frac{P}{P^*}$$

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{\gamma\,\underline{V}_\text{Pt}}{RT\,r}$$

Note: for a **sphere** this would be $2\gamma\underline{V}/RTr$; for a **cylinder** it is $\gamma\underline{V}/RTr$ (one curvature, not two).

**Substituting values** with $r = 5\,\text{nm} = 5 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$:

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{(2.40)(1.011 \times 10^{-5})}{(8.314)(1800)(5 \times 10^{-9})}$$

**Numerator:** $2.40 \times 1.011 \times 10^{-5} = 2.426 \times 10^{-5}$

**Denominator:** $8.314 \times 1800 \times 5 \times 10^{-9} = 7.483 \times 10^{-5}$

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{2.426 \times 10^{-5}}{7.483 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.3242$$

$$\frac{P}{P^*} = e^{0.3242} = 1.383$$

$$\boxed{\frac{P}{P^*} \approx 1.38 \quad (r = 5\,\text{nm})}$$

The 5 nm nanowire has a vapour pressure **38% higher** than the flat bulk surface.

---

### Part (c) — Absolute vapour pressure over the nanowire

$$P = 1.383 \times P^* = 1.383 \times 1.20 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{atm}$$

$$\boxed{P \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{atm}}$$

---

### Part (d) — Ostwald ripening of two nanowire samples

**For S2** with $r_2 = 50\,\text{nm} = 5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{m}$:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P^*} = \frac{(2.40)(1.011 \times 10^{-5})}{(8.314)(1800)(5 \times 10^{-8})} = \frac{2.426 \times 10^{-5}}{7.483 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.03242$$

$$\frac{P_2}{P^*} = e^{0.03242} \approx 1.033$$

$$\boxed{\frac{P_2}{P^*} \approx 1.033 \quad (r = 50\,\text{nm})}$$

S2 has a vapour pressure only **3.3% above** the flat surface, while S1 (5 nm) is **38% above**.

**Physical consequence — Ostwald ripening / coarsening:**

From the Kelvin equation, the equilibrium vapour pressure in the gas phase surrounding S1 ($1.66 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{atm}$) is higher than the equilibrium vapour pressure surrounding S2 ($1.24 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{atm}$):

$$\Delta P_\text{vapour} = P_1 - P_2 = (1.383 - 1.033) \times 1.20 \times 10^{-5} = 4.2 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{atm}$$

This gradient means:
- Pt atoms **evaporate preferentially** from the smaller (higher-$\mu$) nanowire S1.
- The Pt vapour diffuses through the gas phase toward S2, where the vapour pressure is lower and **condensation** is thermodynamically favoured.
- S1 **shrinks**; S2 **grows**.
- The driving force is the difference in chemical potential: $\Delta\mu = RT\ln(P_1/P_2) = 8.314 \times 1800 \times \ln(1.383/1.033) = 14{,}965 \times 0.292 \approx 4{,}370\,\text{J/mol}$.

This is the nanoscale analogue of **grain coarsening / Ostwald ripening**: finer features have higher chemical potential due to surface curvature and are consumed in favour of coarser features. The effect scales as $1/r$, so it becomes negligible for wires above ~1 μm but is highly significant below ~50 nm.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $\underline{V}_\text{Pt} = 1.011 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}$; (b) $P/P^* = 1.38$ for $r = 5\,\text{nm}$; (c) $P = 1.66 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{atm}$; (d) $P/P^* = 1.033$ for $r = 50\,\text{nm}$; S1 evaporates and S2 grows (Ostwald ripening), with a chemical potential driving force of $\approx 4{,}370\,\text{J/mol}$.
common_mistakes: Using the spherical Kelvin equation ($2\gamma/r$) instead of the cylindrical form ($\gamma/r$), which overestimates the vapour pressure enhancement by exactly a factor of 2.
Forgetting to convert the nanowire radius from nm to m before substituting, leading to an answer that is $10^9$ times too large for $\ln(P/P^*)$.

Concluding that because both $P/P^* > 1$ the system is 'not at equilibrium and both samples evaporate equally' — the key insight is the *difference* in vapour pressure between S1 and S2, which drives directional mass transfer from the smaller to the larger wire (Ostwald ripening), not uniform evaporation.

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure of Zinc and the Clausius-Clapeyron Equation
L4|hard.statement:
Zinc (Zn) has a normal boiling point of $1180\,\text{K}$ at $1\,\text{atm}$ and a standard enthalpy of vaporisation $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 115.3\,\text{kJ/mol}$. Assume $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ is independent of temperature.

**(a)** Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, calculate the vapour pressure of liquid zinc at $1000\,\text{K}$ (in atm).

**(b)** A small sealed furnace contains liquid zinc in equilibrium with its own vapour. The furnace is initially at $1000\,\text{K}$. An inert gas (argon, Ar) is then injected into the furnace, raising the total pressure on the liquid surface by $\Delta P = 50\,\text{atm}$ above the original vapour pressure, while the temperature is held constant at $1000\,\text{K}$. Calculate the new equilibrium vapour pressure of zinc under this additional mechanical pressure.

**Data:** $R = 8.314\,\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$; molar mass of Zn $= 65.38\,\text{g/mol}$; density of liquid Zn at $1000\,\text{K}$ $\approx 6.57\,\text{g/cm}^3$.
L4|hard.solution:
## Step 1 — Write the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates the vapour pressure at two temperatures:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

Here we know the reference point: $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$ at $T_1 = 1180\,\text{K}$ (the normal boiling point). We want $P_2$ at $T_2 = 1000\,\text{K}$.

## Part (a)

**Step 2 — Substitute values:**

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{1\,\text{atm}} = -\frac{115{,}300}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{1000} - \frac{1}{1180}\right)$$

Compute the bracket:

$$\frac{1}{1000} - \frac{1}{1180} = 1.000\times10^{-3} - 8.475\times10^{-4} = 1.525\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

Compute the prefactor:

$$\frac{115{,}300}{8.314} = 13{,}869\,\text{K}$$

So:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{1} = -13{,}869 \times 1.525\times10^{-4} = -2.115$$

**Step 3 — Solve for $P_2$:**

$$P_2 = e^{-2.115} \approx 0.121\,\text{atm}$$

$$\boxed{P_\text{vap}(1000\,\text{K}) \approx 0.121\,\text{atm}}$$

This makes physical sense: below the normal boiling point, the vapour pressure must be less than 1 atm. $\checkmark$

---

## Part (b) — Effect of external (mechanical) pressure on vapour pressure

When an inert gas applies extra mechanical pressure $\Delta P$ to the liquid surface, the liquid's chemical potential is raised, which in turn increases the equilibrium vapour pressure. This is the Kelvin pressure effect (also called the Poynting effect for condensed phases).

**Step 4 — Recall the governing equation (L4 §4.10):**

At equilibrium, the chemical potential of the liquid equals that of the vapour. With additional pressure $\Delta P$ on the liquid:

$$V_\text{liq}\,\Delta P = RT\,\ln\frac{P}{P^*}$$

where $P^*$ is the vapour pressure without the extra mechanical pressure (i.e. $P^* = 0.121\,\text{atm}$ from part (a)), and $P$ is the new vapour pressure.

**Step 5 — Compute the molar volume of liquid zinc:**

$$V_\text{liq} = \frac{M_\text{Zn}}{\rho} = \frac{65.38\,\text{g/mol}}{6.57\,\text{g/cm}^3} = 9.952\,\text{cm}^3/\text{mol} = 9.952\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}$$

**Step 6 — Convert $\Delta P$ to SI units:**

$$\Delta P = 50\,\text{atm} = 50 \times 1.013\times10^{5}\,\text{Pa} = 5.065\times10^{6}\,\text{Pa}$$

**Step 7 — Compute $\ln(P/P^*)$:**

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{V_\text{liq}\,\Delta P}{RT} = \frac{9.952\times10^{-6} \times 5.065\times10^{6}}{8.314 \times 1000}$$

$$= \frac{50.41}{8314} = 6.063\times10^{-3}$$

**Step 8 — Solve for $P$:**

$$\frac{P}{P^*} = e^{6.063\times10^{-3}} \approx 1.00608$$

$$P = 1.00608 \times 0.121\,\text{atm} \approx 0.1217\,\text{atm}$$

$$\boxed{P_\text{new} \approx 0.1217\,\text{atm}}$$

The new vapour pressure is only **~0.6% higher** than without the additional pressure. This is entirely typical for condensed phases — liquids barely compress, so even 50 atm of mechanical pressure changes the vapour pressure by less than 1%. Compare this to an ideal gas under the same treatment (where $\mu$ is a strong function of $P$): the effect is orders of magnitude smaller for liquids.

---

## Sanity checks

- **Part (a):** $P_\text{vap} < 1\,\text{atm}$ at $T < T_\text{boil}$ ✓; the result (0.121 atm) places zinc well below its boiling point at 1000 K. ✓
- **Part (b):** The correction is tiny and positive — squeezing liquid always *raises* vapour pressure. $\checkmark$ The small magnitude reflects the fact that $V_\text{liq} \ll V_\text{gas}$. ✓
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $P_\text{vap}(1000\,\text{K}) \approx 0.121\,\text{atm}$; (b) $P_\text{new} \approx 0.1217\,\text{atm}$ (an increase of ~0.6% due to the 50 atm mechanical overpressure from the inert gas).
common_mistakes: **Using the wrong reference point in Clausius-Clapeyron.** Students often set $T_1 = 298\,\text{K}$ and look for a $P$ at 298 K, or forget that the *normal boiling point* is the natural reference ($P = 1\,\text{atm}$ at $T_\text{boil}$). The reference is the boiling point, not standard state.

**Forgetting to convert $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ to J/mol before dividing by $R$ in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.** Using 115.3 kJ/mol directly without multiplying by 1000 gives an answer that is 1000× too small, i.e. a nonsensically tiny $\Delta\ln P$.

**Confusing the Poynting (mechanical pressure) effect with the Clausius-Clapeyron (temperature) effect in part (b).** Students sometimes try to apply the Clausius-Clapeyron equation to part (b), varying temperature, but the temperature is held constant at 1000 K. The correct equation is $V_\text{liq}\,\Delta P = RT\ln(P/P^*)$, which accounts for the extra chemical potential imparted to the liquid by the mechanical pressure of the inert gas.

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure of Liquid Indium Near Its Melting Point
L4|hard.statement:
Liquid indium (In) is used in high-vacuum brazing applications. A process engineer needs to determine how sensitive the equilibrium vapour pressure of liquid indium is to small changes in temperature near the normal boiling point, and then use that sensitivity to predict the vapour pressure at a slightly different operating temperature.

The following data for indium are provided:
- Normal boiling point: $T_b = 2345\,\text{K}$ (at $P^* = 1\,\text{atm}$)
- Molar enthalpy of vaporisation at the normal boiling point: $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 231.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (treat as constant over the temperature range of interest)
- $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

**(a)** Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, write down the expression for $\mathrm{d}\ln P / \mathrm{d}T$ at the normal boiling point ($T = 2345\,\text{K}$, $P = 1\,\text{atm}$) and evaluate it numerically. Express your answer in $\text{K}^{-1}$.

**(b)** The operating furnace temperature is $T_2 = 2295\,\text{K}$ — that is, $50\,\text{K}$ below the normal boiling point. Using the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation, calculate the equilibrium vapour pressure $P_2$ of liquid indium at $T_2$. Express your answer in atm.

**(c)** The engineer claims: *"Since the vapour pressure dropped, the liquid–vapour phase boundary must have a negative slope on the $P$–$T$ diagram at this point, meaning $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T < 0$."* Evaluate this claim using the full Clapeyron equation and the data below, and state whether the claim is correct.

Additional data for part (c):
- Molar volume of liquid In at $T_b$: $\underline{V}_\text{liq} = 17.0\,\text{cm}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}$
- Molar volume of In vapour at $T_b$ (treat as ideal gas): to be calculated from $PV = RT$
- $1\,\text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}$
L4|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Evaluating $\mathrm{d}\ln P / \mathrm{d}T$ at the normal boiling point

The Clausius–Clapeyron equation is:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{RT^2}$$

This is derived from the full Clapeyron equation by (i) approximating $\Delta_\text{vap}V \approx V_\text{gas}$ (neglecting the molar volume of the liquid relative to the gas) and (ii) treating the vapour as ideal so $V_\text{gas} = RT/P$.

Substituting at $T = T_b = 2345\,\text{K}$:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln P}{\mathrm{d}T}\bigg|_{2345\,\text{K}} = \frac{231{,}800\,\text{J mol}^{-1}}{(8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(2345\,\text{K})^2}$$

Compute the denominator:
$$8.314 \times (2345)^2 = 8.314 \times 5{,}499{,}025 = 4.572 \times 10^7\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

Therefore:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{2.318 \times 10^5}{4.572 \times 10^7} = \boxed{5.07 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{K}^{-1}}$$

Physical sense check: a positive value means $\ln P$ (and therefore $P$) increases as $T$ increases — correct for any normal liquid-vapour boundary.

---

## Part (b) — Equilibrium vapour pressure at $T_2 = 2295\,\text{K}$

The integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation (with $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ constant) is:
$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

Here $T_1 = 2345\,\text{K}$, $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$, $T_2 = 2295\,\text{K}$.

**Step 1 — compute the bracket:**
$$\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{2295} - \frac{1}{2345}$$
$$= 4.3573 \times 10^{-4} - 4.2644 \times 10^{-4} = 9.29 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Step 2 — compute the prefactor:**
$$-\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R} = -\frac{231{,}800}{8.314} = -2.788 \times 10^4\,\text{K}$$

**Step 3 — compute $\ln(P_2/P_1)$:**
$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = (-2.788 \times 10^4) \times (9.29 \times 10^{-6}) = -0.2590$$

**Step 4 — solve for $P_2$:**
$$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = e^{-0.2590} = 0.7719$$
$$\boxed{P_2 = 0.772\,\text{atm}}$$

The vapour pressure drops from 1 atm to about 0.77 atm when the temperature falls 50 K below the normal boiling point. This is physically expected: at lower temperature, the liquid is less prone to vaporise, so a lower pressure is needed to maintain phase equilibrium.

---

## Part (c) — Sign of $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T$ from the full Clapeyron equation

The engineer's claim is that $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T < 0$ on the liquid–vapour boundary. We evaluate this using the **exact Clapeyron equation**:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta_\text{vap}S}{\Delta_\text{vap}V} = \frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{T_b\,\Delta_\text{vap}V}$$

**Step 1 — molar volume of vapour (ideal gas at $T_b$, $P = 1\,\text{atm}$):**
$$\underline{V}_\text{gas} = \frac{RT_b}{P} = \frac{(8.314)(2345)}{1.013 \times 10^5}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$
$$= \frac{19{,}496}{1.013 \times 10^5} = 0.1925\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1} = 1.925 \times 10^5\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

**Step 2 — molar volume change on vaporisation:**
$$\Delta_\text{vap}V = \underline{V}_\text{gas} - \underline{V}_\text{liq} = 1.925 \times 10^5 - 17.0 \approx 1.924 \times 10^5\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

Converting to SI: $\Delta_\text{vap}V = 0.1924\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$ (the liquid volume is negligible, as expected for any normal liquid–vapour transition).

**Step 3 — apply the Clapeyron equation:**
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{T_b\,\Delta_\text{vap}V} = \frac{231{,}800\,\text{J mol}^{-1}}{(2345\,\text{K})(0.1924\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1})}$$
$$= \frac{231{,}800}{451.0} = \boxed{514\,\text{Pa K}^{-1} \approx 5.08 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm K}^{-1}}$$

**Conclusion:** $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T = +514\,\text{Pa K}^{-1} > 0$.

**The engineer's claim is WRONG.** The liquid–vapour phase boundary for indium has a *positive* slope on the $P$–$T$ diagram, as it does for every normal substance. The slope is positive because:
- $\Delta H_\text{vap} > 0$ (vaporisation is endothermic — always true)
- $\Delta_\text{vap}V > 0$ (gas occupies far more volume than liquid — always true for normal fluids)

The engineer confused *the direction of the change* (going to lower $T$ lowers $P$, tracing backward along a positively-sloped curve) with the *sign of the slope*. A positive $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T$ means $P$ decreases when $T$ decreases — which is exactly what part (b) showed. There is no contradiction.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $\mathrm{d}\ln P/\mathrm{d}T = 5.07 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{K}^{-1}$; (b) $P_2 = 0.772\,\text{atm}$; (c) $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T = +514\,\text{Pa K}^{-1} > 0$ — the engineer's claim is incorrect; the slope is positive.
common_mistakes: Inverting the bracket in the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation: writing $(1/T_1 - 1/T_2)$ instead of $(1/T_2 - 1/T_1)$ and getting $P_2 > 1\,\text{atm}$, which contradicts physics (lower $T$ should give lower vapour pressure for a normal fluid).

In part (c), forgetting to subtract the liquid molar volume from the gas molar volume when computing $\Delta_\text{vap}V$, or (more commonly) using $\Delta_\text{vap}V = \underline{V}_\text{liq}$ instead of $\underline{V}_\text{gas} - \underline{V}_\text{liq}$.

Claiming that because $P_2 < P_1$ the slope $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T$ must be negative — confusing the direction of traversal along the phase boundary (we moved to lower $T$ and lower $P$) with the sign of the slope (which is positive because both $T$ and $P$ decrease together).

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure Enhancement of Nano-Iron Droplets via Surface Tension
L4|hard.statement:
During a gas-phase synthesis process, liquid iron droplets of radius $r = 5\,\text{nm}$ are produced at $T = 1873\,\text{K}$ (just above the melting point of iron at 1 atm). The equilibrium vapour pressure of bulk liquid iron (flat surface) at this temperature is $P^* = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$.

**Given data:**
- Surface tension of liquid iron: $\gamma = 1.87\,\text{N m}^{-1}$
- Molar mass of iron: $M = 55.85\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$
- Density of liquid iron at 1873 K: $\rho = 7.0 \times 10^3\,\text{kg m}^{-3}$
- Gas constant: $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$

**(a)** Calculate the molar volume $V_\text{liq}$ of liquid iron at 1873 K.

**(b)** Using the Kelvin equation, calculate the equilibrium vapour pressure $P$ of the 5 nm iron droplet. By what percentage does the vapour pressure of the nano-droplet exceed that of bulk iron at the same temperature?

**(c)** In the same synthesis reactor, both 5 nm droplets and 50 nm droplets of liquid iron are present simultaneously. Using the Kelvin equation, explain qualitatively and quantitatively what thermodynamic driving force exists between the two droplet populations, and predict the direction of mass transfer. Which population will grow and which will shrink?
L4|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Molar volume of liquid iron

The molar volume is defined as:
$$V_\text{liq} = \frac{M}{\rho}$$

Substituting values (converting $M$ to kg mol$^{-1}$):
$$V_\text{liq} = \frac{55.85 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg mol}^{-1}}{7.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}} = 7.98 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{V_\text{liq} = 7.98 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}}$$

---

### Part (b) — Kelvin equation for the 5 nm droplet

The **Kelvin equation** (derived in L4 from the mechanical equilibrium of a curved liquid surface with the Laplace pressure $\Delta P = 2\gamma/r$, substituted into the mechanical pressure—vapour pressure relation for a liquid) is:

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{2\gamma V_\text{liq}}{RT\, r}$$

**Identify all quantities:**
- $\gamma = 1.87\,\text{N m}^{-1}$
- $V_\text{liq} = 7.98 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}$
- $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
- $T = 1873\,\text{K}$
- $r = 5\,\text{nm} = 5 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$

**Compute the exponent:**
$$\frac{2\gamma V_\text{liq}}{RT\, r} = \frac{2 \times 1.87 \times 7.98 \times 10^{-6}}{8.314 \times 1873 \times 5 \times 10^{-9}}$$

**Numerator:** $2 \times 1.87 \times 7.98 \times 10^{-6} = 2.985 \times 10^{-5}$

**Denominator:** $8.314 \times 1873 \times 5 \times 10^{-9} = 7.784 \times 10^{-5}$

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{2.985 \times 10^{-5}}{7.784 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.3835$$

**Solve for $P$:**
$$\frac{P}{P^*} = e^{0.3835} = 1.467$$

$$P = 1.467 \times 4.2 \times 10^{-3} = 6.16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$$

$$\boxed{P_{r=5\,\text{nm}} = 6.16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}}$$

**Percentage enhancement:**
$$\text{Enhancement} = (1.467 - 1) \times 100\% = \mathbf{46.7\%}$$

The 5 nm droplet has a vapour pressure approximately **47% higher** than bulk liquid iron at 1873 K.

---

### Part (c) — Coarsening direction between 5 nm and 50 nm droplets

Apply the Kelvin equation to the 50 nm droplet:

$$\ln\frac{P_{50}}{P^*} = \frac{2\gamma V_\text{liq}}{RT\, r_{50}} = \frac{2 \times 1.87 \times 7.98 \times 10^{-6}}{8.314 \times 1873 \times 50 \times 10^{-9}}$$

**Denominator** for 50 nm: $8.314 \times 1873 \times 50 \times 10^{-9} = 7.784 \times 10^{-4}$

$$\ln\frac{P_{50}}{P^*} = \frac{2.985 \times 10^{-5}}{7.784 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.03835$$

$$P_{50} = P^* \times e^{0.03835} = 4.2 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.039 = 4.36 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$$

**Summary of vapour pressures:**

| Droplet radius | Vapour pressure (atm) | Enhancement over bulk |
|---|---|---|
| 5 nm | $6.16 \times 10^{-3}$ | +46.7% |
| 50 nm | $4.36 \times 10^{-3}$ | +3.9% |
| Bulk (flat) | $4.20 \times 10^{-3}$ | 0% |

**Thermodynamic driving force:**

The vapour pressure of the 5 nm droplet ($6.16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$) exceeds that of the 50 nm droplet ($4.36 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$) by:
$$\Delta P = (6.16 - 4.36) \times 10^{-3} = 1.80 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$$

Since chemical potential increases with vapour pressure (from $\mu = \mu^\circ + RT\ln P$ for an ideal vapour), and the 5 nm droplets have higher $\mu$ than the 50 nm droplets, iron atoms in the gas phase near 5 nm droplets are at higher chemical potential than those near 50 nm droplets.

**Direction of mass transfer:** Iron evaporates preferentially from the small (5 nm) droplets and condenses onto the large (50 nm) droplets. The **5 nm droplets shrink and eventually disappear; the 50 nm droplets grow**.

This is **Ostwald ripening** (coarsening): curvature-driven mass transfer from small high-$\mu$ particles to large low-$\mu$ particles, entirely driven by the surface-energy term captured in the Kelvin equation. The thermodynamic driving force is the difference in chemical potential:
$$\Delta\mu = RT\ln\frac{P_{5}}{P_{50}} = 8.314 \times 1873 \times \ln\frac{6.16}{4.36} = 8.314 \times 1873 \times 0.346 = 5{,}387\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

This $\sim 5.4\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ difference is the molar driving force for iron to transfer from 5 nm to 50 nm droplets.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $V_\text{liq} = 7.98 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}$; (b) $P_{5\,\text{nm}} = 6.16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$, a 46.7% enhancement over bulk; (c) $\Delta\mu \approx 5.4\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ drives Ostwald ripening: 5 nm droplets evaporate and shrink, 50 nm droplets grow.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert the droplet radius from nm to m before substituting into the Kelvin equation — using $r = 5$ instead of $r = 5\times10^{-9}$ m inflates the exponent by $10^9$ and gives a physically absurd vapour pressure enhancement.

Confusing which droplet has higher vapour pressure: students sometimes reason that 'larger droplets have more surface area therefore higher vapour pressure.' The Kelvin equation depends on curvature ($1/r$), not total area — smaller radius means higher curvature, higher Laplace pressure, and higher vapour pressure.

Applying the Kelvin equation with $\Delta P = 2\gamma/r$ directly as a vapour pressure correction (adding it to $P^*$) rather than using the logarithmic form $\ln(P/P^*) = 2\gamma V_\text{liq}/(RTr)$. The linear approximation breaks down for very small droplets where the exponent is not small.

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure of Liquid Sodium at High Temperature
L4|hard.statement:
Liquid sodium (Na) is used as a coolant in certain fast-breeder nuclear reactors. A safety engineer needs to estimate the vapour pressure of sodium above the liquid at 1200 K to assess the risk of Na vapour release.

The following thermodynamic data are available for sodium:

**Normal boiling point:** $T_b = 1156$ K at $P^* = 1$ atm

**Standard enthalpy of vaporisation:** $\Delta H^\circ_\text{vap} = 89{,}040$ J mol$^{-1}$ (treat as approximately constant over this temperature range)

**Gas constant:** $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

**(a)** Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, calculate the equilibrium vapour pressure of liquid sodium at 1200 K. Express your answer in atm and in Pa.

**(b)** At 1200 K, the liquid sodium is exposed to an inert argon gas blanket maintained at a total pressure of 3 atm. Using the Kelvin equation, determine the fractional increase in the sodium vapour pressure $(P - P^*_\text{Na}) / P^*_\text{Na}$ caused by the mechanical pressure of the argon gas, where $P^*_\text{Na}$ is the answer from part (a).

**Additional data for part (b):**
- Molar mass of Na: $M = 22.99$ g mol$^{-1}$
- Liquid density of Na at 1200 K: $\rho = 800$ kg m$^{-3}$
- The mechanical overpressure $\Delta P$ on the liquid from the argon blanket equals the argon partial pressure: $\Delta P = P_\text{total} - P^*_\text{Na}$ (approximate as $\approx 3$ atm since $P^*_\text{Na} \ll 3$ atm)
- $1$ atm $= 1.013 \times 10^5$ Pa
L4|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Clausius-Clapeyron to find vapour pressure at 1200 K

**Step 1 — Identify the governing equation.**

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates the vapour pressure at two temperatures:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

Here: $P_1 = 1$ atm at $T_1 = 1156$ K (normal boiling point); $T_2 = 1200$ K; solve for $P_2$.

**Step 2 — Compute the bracket.**

$$\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{1200} - \frac{1}{1156} = 8.3333 \times 10^{-4} - 8.6505 \times 10^{-4} = -3.172 \times 10^{-5}\;\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Step 3 — Compute $\ln(P_2/P_1)$.**

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{89{,}040}{8.314} \times (-3.172 \times 10^{-5})$$

$$= 10{,}710.6 \times 3.172 \times 10^{-5} = +0.3397$$

**Step 4 — Find $P_2$.**

$$P_2 = P_1 \times e^{0.3397} = 1 \times 1.404 = \boxed{1.404\;\text{atm}}$$

Converting to Pa:

$$P_2 = 1.404 \times 1.013 \times 10^5 = 1.422 \times 10^5\;\text{Pa}$$

**Sanity check:** $T_2 = 1200$ K $> T_b = 1156$ K, so the vapour pressure should exceed 1 atm. We get 1.404 atm $> 1$ atm. ✓ The fractional increase per kelvin above the boiling point is consistent with the Trouton's-rule-level $\Delta H_\text{vap}$.

---

## Part (b) — Kelvin equation for mechanical pressure effect

**Step 1 — Recall the Kelvin (mechanical pressure) equation.**

When an external mechanical pressure $\Delta P$ is applied to a condensed (liquid) phase, the equilibrium vapour pressure rises by:

$$V_\text{liq}\,\Delta P = RT\,\ln\frac{P}{P^*_\text{Na}}$$

where $V_\text{liq}$ is the molar volume of the liquid and $P^*_\text{Na}$ is the vapour pressure without the extra mechanical pressure (from part (a)).

**Step 2 — Compute the molar volume of liquid sodium at 1200 K.**

$$V_\text{liq} = \frac{M}{\rho} = \frac{22.99 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{kg mol}^{-1}}{800\;\text{kg m}^{-3}} = 2.874 \times 10^{-5}\;\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

**Step 3 — Compute the mechanical overpressure $\Delta P$.**

The argon blanket applies a total pressure of 3 atm. Since the Na vapour pressure is $\approx 1.4$ atm and the inert Ar does not condense, the mechanical pressure acting on the liquid surface equals the total pressure:

$$\Delta P \approx 3\;\text{atm} = 3 \times 1.013 \times 10^5 = 3.039 \times 10^5\;\text{Pa}$$

(The problem states to approximate $\Delta P \approx 3$ atm for simplicity.)

**Step 4 — Compute $\ln(P/P^*_\text{Na})$.**

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*_\text{Na}} = \frac{V_\text{liq}\,\Delta P}{RT} = \frac{(2.874 \times 10^{-5})(3.039 \times 10^5)}{(8.314)(1200)}$$

$$= \frac{8.734}{9{,}977} = 8.754 \times 10^{-4}$$

**Step 5 — Compute the fractional increase.**

For small $x$, $\ln(1 + x) \approx x$, so:

$$\frac{P - P^*_\text{Na}}{P^*_\text{Na}} = e^{8.754 \times 10^{-4}} - 1 \approx 8.754 \times 10^{-4} \approx \boxed{0.0876\%}$$

**Interpretation:** A 3 atm argon blanket raises the sodium vapour pressure by less than 0.09%. This is negligibly small — consistent with the general principle that mechanical pressure has very little effect on the vapour pressure of a liquid (since $V_\text{liq}$ is tiny). The dominant factor controlling Na vapour pressure is temperature, not the argon blanket pressure. This justifies the common engineering assumption that inert-gas blankets in reactor systems do not substantially alter coolant evaporation rates.
common_mistakes: **Inverting the bracket in Clausius-Clapeyron:** Writing $(1/T_1 - 1/T_2)$ instead of $(1/T_2 - 1/T_1)$ flips the sign of $\ln(P_2/P_1)$, giving a vapour pressure below 1 atm at a temperature above the boiling point — a physically impossible result that students often miss.

**Confusing the Clausius-Clapeyron equation with the Kelvin (capillary) equation:** The Clausius-Clapeyron equation gives vapour pressure as a function of temperature via latent heat; the Kelvin equation gives the additional effect of mechanical pressure on the liquid. Students sometimes try to use one equation for both parts, leading to nonsensical results.

**Forgetting to convert $\Delta P$ to Pa in part (b):** The Kelvin equation $V_\text{liq}\,\Delta P = RT\ln(P/P^*)$ requires SI units throughout ($V$ in m$^3$ mol$^{-1}$, $\Delta P$ in Pa, $R$ in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). Leaving $\Delta P$ in atm without conversion gives an answer $\sim 10^5$ times too small.

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure of Liquid Titanium Near Its Boiling Point
L4|hard.statement:
Titanium metal boils at $T_b = 3560\,\text{K}$ at 1 atm, with a standard molar enthalpy of vaporisation $\Delta H^\circ_\text{vap} = 427{,}000\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$ (treat as constant over the temperature range of interest). A vacuum arc-melting furnace maintains a chamber pressure of $P_\text{chamber} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$.

**(a)** Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, determine the temperature $T_2$ at which liquid titanium is in equilibrium with its vapour at the chamber pressure $2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$ (i.e., the effective boiling point inside the furnace).

**(b)** A small spherical droplet of liquid titanium of radius $r = 5\,\text{nm}$ is suspended in the furnace at the temperature $T_2$ found in part (a). Given that the surface tension of liquid titanium is $\gamma = 1.65\,\text{N m}^{-1}$ and the molar volume of liquid titanium is $V_\text{liq} = 10.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}$, calculate the equilibrium vapour pressure above this droplet using the Kelvin equation and compare it with the flat-surface equilibrium vapour pressure $P^* = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$.

**(c)** State whether the nanodroplet is stable in the furnace atmosphere and explain the physical consequence in terms of droplet evaporation.

Use $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
L4|hard.solution:
## Part (a) — Effective boiling point at reduced pressure

**Equation:** The Clausius–Clapeyron equation (integrated form, assuming $\Delta H^\circ_\text{vap}$ constant):

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

**Known values:**
- $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$, $T_1 = 3560\,\text{K}$ (normal boiling point)
- $P_2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$
- $\Delta H^\circ_\text{vap} = 427{,}000\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$
- $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

**Step 1 — Compute the left-hand side:**

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \ln\left(2.0 \times 10^{-3}\right) = \ln(2.0) + \ln(10^{-3}) = 0.693 - 6.908 = -6.215$$

**Step 2 — Rearrange for $1/T_2$:**

$$-6.215 = -\frac{427{,}000}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{3560}\right)$$

$$-6.215 = -51{,}362\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - 2.809 \times 10^{-4}\right)$$

$$\frac{1}{T_2} - 2.809 \times 10^{-4} = \frac{6.215}{51{,}362} = 1.210 \times 10^{-4}$$

$$\frac{1}{T_2} = 2.809 \times 10^{-4} + 1.210 \times 10^{-4} = 4.019 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{T_2 = \frac{1}{4.019 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 2488\,\text{K}}$$

The effective boiling point of titanium in the vacuum furnace is approximately **2488 K** — about 1072 K below the atmospheric boiling point. This is why vacuum arc melting can process titanium at a meaningfully lower temperature.

---

## Part (b) — Vapour pressure above a 5 nm droplet via the Kelvin equation

**Equation (Kelvin equation):**

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{2\gamma V_\text{liq}}{RT_2\, r}$$

**Known values at $T_2 = 2488\,\text{K}$:**
- $\gamma = 1.65\,\text{N m}^{-1}$
- $V_\text{liq} = 10.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1}$
- $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
- $T_2 = 2488\,\text{K}$
- $r = 5\,\text{nm} = 5 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$
- $P^* = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$

**Step 1 — Evaluate the numerator:**

$$2\gamma V_\text{liq} = 2 \times 1.65 \times 10.6 \times 10^{-6} = 3.498 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{N m}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^3\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 3.498 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{m}$$

**Step 2 — Evaluate the denominator:**

$$RT_2\, r = 8.314 \times 2488 \times 5 \times 10^{-9} = 8.314 \times 2488 = 20{,}685\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$
$$20{,}685 \times 5 \times 10^{-9} = 1.034 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{m}$$

**Step 3 — Compute $\ln(P/P^*)$:**

$$\ln\frac{P}{P^*} = \frac{3.498 \times 10^{-5}}{1.034 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.3383$$

**Step 4 — Solve for $P$:**

$$\frac{P}{P^*} = e^{0.3383} \approx 1.402$$

$$\boxed{P = 1.402 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3} = 2.80 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}}$$

The equilibrium vapour pressure above the 5 nm droplet is approximately **$2.80 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$**, which is **40% higher** than the flat-surface value $P^* = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$.

---

## Part (c) — Stability of the nanodroplet

The furnace chamber is maintained at $P_\text{chamber} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$.

The equilibrium vapour pressure *above the droplet* is $P_\text{droplet} = 2.80 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$.

Since $P_\text{droplet} > P_\text{chamber}$, the vapour immediately surrounding the droplet has a higher equilibrium pressure than the chamber. Titanium vapour therefore flows **away from** the droplet surface into the lower-pressure chamber environment — the droplet **evaporates spontaneously**.

Physically, the high Laplace pressure inside the small droplet raises the chemical potential of the liquid titanium above that of a flat surface, which in turn requires a higher vapour pressure for equilibrium. Since the chamber cannot sustain that elevated vapour pressure (it is held at the flat-surface value), the droplet is thermodynamically unstable and will shrink by evaporation. This is entirely analogous to Ostwald ripening in solid systems: small particles/droplets dissolve (evaporate) while large ones grow, because small curvature means elevated chemical potential.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $T_2 \approx 2488\,\text{K}$; (b) $P_\text{droplet} \approx 2.80 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{atm}$ (about 40% above the flat-surface value); (c) the nanodroplet is unstable and evaporates because its equilibrium vapour pressure exceeds the chamber pressure.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert the droplet radius from nanometres to metres before substituting into the Kelvin equation, causing the argument of the logarithm to be wrong by a factor of $10^9$.

In the Clausius–Clapeyron step, computing $\ln(P_2/P_1)$ as $\ln(P_1/P_2)$ (reversing the ratio), which gives a boiling-point elevation instead of the correct depression — always check that lower pressure should give lower boiling point.

Confusing the flat-surface equilibrium vapour pressure $P^*$ (used as the reference in the Kelvin equation) with the chamber operating pressure; they happen to be equal here by construction, but students must recognise that $P^*$ is the thermodynamic reference for a flat liquid surface at $T_2$, not an independently set quantity.

L4|hard.title: Clausius-Clapeyron Analysis of Sulphur Solid-Solid Transition
L4|hard.statement:
Sulphur exists in two solid allotropic forms: rhombic sulphur ($\alpha$-S) and monoclinic sulphur ($\beta$-S). At atmospheric pressure (1 atm $= 1.013 \times 10^5$ Pa), the transition temperature is $T_\text{trs} = 368.5$ K. The following thermodynamic data are available at this transition:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $\Delta H_\text{trs}$ ($\alpha \to \beta$) | $+401$ J mol$^{-1}$ |
| Density of $\alpha$-S | $2.07$ g cm$^{-3}$ |
| Density of $\beta$-S | $1.96$ g cm$^{-3}$ |
| Molar mass of S | $32.06$ g mol$^{-1}$ |

**(a)** Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S_\text{trs}$ for the $\alpha \to \beta$ transition at 368.5 K.

**(b)** Compute the molar volume change $\Delta V_\text{trs} = V_\beta - V_\alpha$ in m$^3$ mol$^{-1}$.

**(c)** Using the Clapeyron equation, calculate the slope $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T$ of the $\alpha$–$\beta$ phase boundary in Pa K$^{-1}$.

**(d)** A high-pressure apparatus imposes an external pressure of $P = 4.0 \times 10^7$ Pa (approximately 395 atm) on the sulphur sample. Using the slope computed in (c) and assuming it is constant, estimate the new $\alpha \to \beta$ transition temperature $T_\text{trs}^\prime$ at this elevated pressure.

**(e)** At the new transition temperature $T_\text{trs}^\prime$, determine the equilibrium vapour pressure ratio $P_\text{vap}(T_\text{trs}^\prime)/P_\text{vap}(368.5\,\text{K})$ for monoclinic sulphur vapourising to S(g), given that the molar enthalpy of vaporisation of $\beta$-S is $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 45{,}000$ J mol$^{-1}$ (treat S vapour as an ideal gas and $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ as constant over the temperature range).
L4|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Entropy change of transition

At a reversible phase transition occurring at constant $T$ and $P$, the Second Law gives:

$$\Delta S_\text{trs} = \frac{\Delta H_\text{trs}}{T_\text{trs}}$$

Substituting:

$$\Delta S_\text{trs} = \frac{+401\,\text{J mol}^{-1}}{368.5\,\text{K}} = +1.088\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

> The positive sign confirms that $\beta$-S (monoclinic) is more disordered than $\alpha$-S (rhombic), as expected for the higher-temperature polymorph.

---

### Part (b) — Molar volume change

Molar volume of each phase:

$$V_\alpha = \frac{M}{\rho_\alpha} = \frac{32.06\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{2.07\,\text{g cm}^{-3}} = 15.49\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1} = 15.49 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

$$V_\beta = \frac{M}{\rho_\beta} = \frac{32.06\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{1.96\,\text{g cm}^{-3}} = 16.36\,\text{cm}^3\text{mol}^{-1} = 16.36 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta V_\text{trs} = V_\beta - V_\alpha = (16.36 - 15.49) \times 10^{-6} = +0.87 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}$$

---

### Part (c) — Clapeyron slope $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T$

The **Clapeyron equation** for a solid–solid boundary is:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta_\text{trs} S}{\Delta_\text{trs} V} = \frac{\Delta_\text{trs} H}{T_\text{trs}\,\Delta_\text{trs} V}$$

Substituting:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{401\,\text{J mol}^{-1}}{368.5\,\text{K} \times 0.87 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}}$$

$$= \frac{401}{3.206 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.251 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa K}^{-1}$$

> Units check: $\text{J mol}^{-1}\,/\,(\text{K}\cdot\text{m}^3\text{mol}^{-1}) = \text{Pa K}^{-1}$ ✓ (since J m$^{-3}$ = Pa).

---

### Part (d) — New transition temperature under high pressure

Assuming the Clapeyron slope is constant, we can write:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} \approx \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta T} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta T = \frac{\Delta P}{\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T}$$

Pressure increase above 1 atm:

$$\Delta P = 4.0 \times 10^7 - 1.013 \times 10^5 \approx 3.99 \times 10^7\,\text{Pa}$$

(The atmospheric pressure is negligible compared to $4.0 \times 10^7$ Pa, so $\Delta P \approx 4.0 \times 10^7$ Pa.)

$$\Delta T = \frac{3.99 \times 10^7\,\text{Pa}}{1.251 \times 10^6\,\text{Pa K}^{-1}} = +31.9\,\text{K}$$

$$T_\text{trs}^\prime = 368.5 + 31.9 = \boxed{400.4\,\text{K}}$$

> **Physical interpretation:** Both $\Delta H_\text{trs} > 0$ and $\Delta V_\text{trs} > 0$, so the Clapeyron slope is positive. Increasing pressure **raises** the $\alpha \to \beta$ transition temperature — unlike the anomalous water case (where $\Delta V < 0$ gives a negative slope). This is the typical solid–solid behaviour.

---

### Part (e) — Vapour pressure ratio via Clausius-Clapeyron

We need $P_\text{vap}(T_\text{trs}^\prime)/P_\text{vap}(368.5\,\text{K})$ for the $\beta$-S to S(g) equilibrium.

The **Clausius-Clapeyron equation** (integrated, assuming $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ constant and vapour is ideal):

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

Here: $T_1 = 368.5$ K, $T_2 = T_\text{trs}^\prime = 400.4$ K, $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 45{,}000$ J mol$^{-1}$, $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

Compute the bracket:

$$\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{400.4} - \frac{1}{368.5} = 2.4975 \times 10^{-3} - 2.7138 \times 10^{-3} = -2.163 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

Then:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{45{,}000}{8.314} \times (-2.163 \times 10^{-4}) = +5412 \times 2.163 \times 10^{-4} = +1.171$$

$$\frac{P_\text{vap}(400.4\,\text{K})}{P_\text{vap}(368.5\,\text{K})} = e^{1.171} \approx \boxed{3.22}$$

> **Interpretation:** The vapour pressure of monoclinic sulphur at the elevated transition temperature is approximately **3.2 times higher** than at 368.5 K. This is physically sensible — a hotter liquid or solid always has a higher vapour pressure, and the exponential sensitivity of vapour pressure to temperature (Clausius-Clapeyron) produces a factor of ~3 for a ~32 K rise with a moderate $\Delta H_\text{vap}$.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S_\text{trs} = +1.088$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; (b) $\Delta V_\text{trs} = +0.87 \times 10^{-6}$ m$^3$ mol$^{-1}$; (c) $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T = 1.251 \times 10^6$ Pa K$^{-1}$; (d) $T_\text{trs}^\prime \approx 400.4$ K; (e) $P_\text{vap}(400.4\,\text{K})/P_\text{vap}(368.5\,\text{K}) \approx 3.22$
common_mistakes: **Forgetting to convert cm³ to m³ for molar volumes.** Using $\Delta V$ in cm$^3$ mol$^{-1}$ without the $10^{-6}$ conversion factor gives a Clapeyron slope 10$^6$ times too small, leading to an absurdly large $\Delta T$ in part (d). Always check that $\Delta V$ is in m$^3$ mol$^{-1}$ so that the slope comes out in Pa K$^{-1}$.

**Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation (for liquid–vapour) instead of the full Clapeyron equation for the solid–solid boundary in parts (a)–(d).** The Clausius-Clapeyron simplification ($\Delta V \approx V_\text{gas} = RT/P$) only applies when one phase is a low-density vapour and the condensed-phase volume is negligible. For a solid–solid transition both phases are dense; you must use the exact Clapeyron equation with the computed $\Delta V_\text{trs}$.

**In part (e), confusing which $T$ is $T_1$ and which is $T_2$ in the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation, causing a sign error.** This flips the ratio to $1/3.22 \approx 0.31$ instead of 3.22. A simple sanity check — higher $T$ must give higher vapour pressure for a substance with positive $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ — immediately reveals the mistake.

L4|hard.title: Clausius-Clapeyron: Vapour Pressure of Liquid Iron at High Temperature
L4|hard.statement:
Molten iron in a vacuum induction furnace operates at elevated temperature, and process engineers must estimate the equilibrium vapour pressure of liquid iron at the furnace operating temperature to assess evaporative losses.

The following data are given for liquid iron:
- Normal boiling point of iron: $T_b = 3134\,\text{K}$ (at $P = 1\,\text{atm}$)
- Molar enthalpy of vaporisation: $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 349{,}600\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$ (treat as constant)
- Universal gas constant: $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

The vacuum furnace operates at $T_\text{op} = 2800\,\text{K}$ (well above the melting point of iron at 1811 K, so iron is fully liquid).

**(a)** Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, calculate the equilibrium vapour pressure of liquid iron at 2800 K. Express your answer in atm.

**(b)** The furnace chamber is backfilled with argon to a total pressure of $0.05\,\text{atm}$. State whether liquid iron will evaporate spontaneously under this condition at 2800 K, justifying your answer thermodynamically using the chemical potential criterion $\mu_\text{liq}$ vs $\mu_\text{gas}$.

**(c)** Find the temperature $T^*$ at which the equilibrium vapour pressure of liquid iron equals exactly $0.05\,\text{atm}$. This is the minimum temperature at which iron will boil in the argon-backfilled chamber.
L4|hard.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Vapour pressure of liquid iron at 2800 K

**Identify the governing equation.** The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates vapour pressure to temperature:

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

**Assign reference and target states.**
- Reference: $(P_1, T_1) = (1\,\text{atm},\; 3134\,\text{K})$ — the normal boiling point.
- Target: $(P_2, T_2) = (P_?\,\text{atm},\; 2800\,\text{K})$.

**Substitute values.**

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{1} = -\frac{349{,}600}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{2800} - \frac{1}{3134}\right)$$

Compute the bracket:
$$\frac{1}{2800} = 3.5714\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}, \qquad \frac{1}{3134} = 3.1908\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$
$$\frac{1}{2800} - \frac{1}{3134} = (3.5714 - 3.1908)\times10^{-4} = 3.806\times10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

Compute the prefactor:
$$\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R} = \frac{349{,}600}{8.314} = 42{,}047\,\text{K}$$

Therefore:
$$\ln P_2 = -42{,}047 \times 3.806\times10^{-5} = -1.6003$$

$$P_2 = e^{-1.6003} = 0.2019\,\text{atm}$$

$$\boxed{P_2 \approx 0.202\,\text{atm}}$$

---

### Part (b) — Will iron evaporate spontaneously at $P_\text{Ar} = 0.05\,\text{atm}$, $T = 2800\,\text{K}$?

**Physical argument using chemical potential.** At a given temperature, the equilibrium vapour pressure $P^*_{\text{eq}}(T)$ is the pressure at which the molar Gibbs energy (chemical potential) of liquid and vapour are equal:

$$\mu_\text{liq}(T,P) = \mu_\text{gas}(T, P^*_\text{eq})$$

From Part (a), $P^*_\text{eq}(2800\,\text{K}) \approx 0.202\,\text{atm}$.

The actual partial pressure of iron vapour in the argon-backfilled chamber is essentially zero initially (argon is inert and provides no iron vapour). The iron vapour pressure above the melt is far below its equilibrium value ($P_\text{Fe,actual} \ll P^*_\text{eq} = 0.202\,\text{atm}$).

For the vaporisation reaction $\text{Fe(l)} \to \text{Fe(g)}$:

$$\Delta G_\text{vap} = \Delta G^\circ_\text{vap} + RT\ln Q$$

where the reaction quotient is $Q = P_\text{Fe,actual}/1\,\text{atm} \approx 0$ (far below equilibrium). Since $Q < K$ (the equilibrium constant corresponds to $P^*_\text{eq} = 0.202\,\text{atm}$), we have $\Delta G_\text{vap} < 0$.

Alternatively: $\mu_\text{gas}(T, P_\text{Fe,actual}) < \mu_\text{gas}(T, P^*_\text{eq}) = \mu_\text{liq}(T)$, so iron spontaneously transfers from liquid to vapour phase to raise the iron vapour pressure toward equilibrium.

**Total argon backfill pressure of 0.05 atm is irrelevant** — argon is inert, does not dissolve in iron, and does not contribute to the iron chemical potential. The driving force for evaporation depends only on the iron vapour partial pressure relative to $P^*_\text{eq}$.

$$\boxed{\text{Yes — liquid iron evaporates spontaneously at 2800 K because }P^*_\text{eq}(2800\,\text{K}) = 0.202\,\text{atm} \gg 0.}$$

---

### Part (c) — Temperature $T^*$ at which $P^*_\text{eq} = 0.05\,\text{atm}$

This is the temperature at which the iron vapour pressure exactly equals the argon backfill pressure, so boiling (bulk vaporisation) commences.

**Apply Clausius-Clapeyron** with:
- $(P_1, T_1) = (1\,\text{atm},\; 3134\,\text{K})$
- $(P_2, T_2) = (0.05\,\text{atm},\; T^*)$

$$\ln\frac{0.05}{1} = -\frac{42{,}047}{1}\left(\frac{1}{T^*} - \frac{1}{3134}\right)$$

$$\ln(0.05) = -2.9957$$

$$-2.9957 = -42{,}047\left(\frac{1}{T^*} - 3.1908\times10^{-4}\right)$$

$$\frac{1}{T^*} - 3.1908\times10^{-4} = \frac{2.9957}{42{,}047} = 7.124\times10^{-5}$$

$$\frac{1}{T^*} = 3.1908\times10^{-4} + 7.124\times10^{-5} = 3.9032\times10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$T^* = \frac{1}{3.9032\times10^{-4}} = 2562\,\text{K}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 2562\,\text{K}\;(\approx 2289\,°\text{C})}$$

**Interpretation.** At the operating temperature of 2800 K, iron is 238 K above the effective boiling point in this reduced-pressure environment. This confirms significant evaporative loss, and explains why vacuum induction furnaces operating above ~2562 K with 0.05 atm Ar backfill suffer measurable iron vapour deposition on cooler chamber walls.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $P^*_\text{eq}(2800\,\text{K}) \approx 0.202\,\text{atm}$; (b) Yes, iron evaporates spontaneously because $P^*_\text{eq} \gg P_\text{Fe,actual}$, giving $\Delta G_\text{vap} < 0$; (c) $T^* \approx 2562\,\text{K}$
common_mistakes: **Using total chamber pressure instead of iron partial pressure.** Students often compare $P^*_\text{eq}$ to the argon backfill pressure (0.05 atm), concluding incorrectly that iron will not evaporate because $P_\text{total} < P^*_\text{eq}$. The equilibrium criterion involves only the partial pressure of iron vapour, not inert gas pressure. Argon is chemically irrelevant to the Fe(l)/Fe(g) equilibrium.

**Sign error in the Clausius-Clapeyron bracket.** The bracket is $(1/T_2 - 1/T_1)$. Students frequently invert this to $(1/T_1 - 1/T_2)$, flipping the sign of $\ln(P_2/P_1)$ and obtaining a vapour pressure greater than 1 atm at 2800 K (i.e. predicting $P_2 > P_1$ when $T_2 < T_1$), which is physically wrong — vapour pressure must decrease as temperature decreases below the normal boiling point.

**Forgetting that $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ must be in J/mol (not kJ/mol) when using $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.** Using 349.6 (kJ) instead of 349 600 (J) gives a ratio $\Delta H/R$ that is 1000 times too small, yielding a negligibly small $\ln(P_2/P_1)$ and an incorrect conclusion that vapour pressure barely changes with temperature.

L4|hard.title: Vapour Pressure of Solid CO₂ (Dry Ice) Near Sublimation
L4|hard.statement:
Carbon dioxide undergoes direct sublimation (solid → gas) without passing through a liquid phase at atmospheric pressure. The following thermodynamic data are available for CO₂ at its standard sublimation point of $T_1 = 194.65\,\text{K}$ (at $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}$):

- Molar enthalpy of sublimation: $\Delta H_{\text{sub}} = 25{,}200\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$
- Molar entropy of sublimation: $\Delta S_{\text{sub}} = 129.4\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
- Molar volume of solid CO₂: $\underline{V}_{\text{solid}} = 28.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$
- Universal gas constant: $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

Answer all three parts:

**(a)** Verify that solid and gaseous CO₂ are in thermodynamic equilibrium at $T_1 = 194.65\,\text{K}$, $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$ by computing $\Delta G_{\text{sub}}$ at these conditions.

**(b)** Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, calculate the equilibrium vapour pressure of solid CO₂ at $T_2 = 170\,\text{K}$. Treat $\Delta H_{\text{sub}}$ as temperature-independent.

**(c)** A sealed rigid container holds only solid CO₂ and its vapour in equilibrium at $T_2 = 170\,\text{K}$. The container is isothermally heated from $170\,\text{K}$ to $194.65\,\text{K}$ while remaining sealed. Using the Maxwell relation derived from the Gibbs free energy, estimate the change in molar entropy of the **gas phase** due to this pressure change at constant temperature. Treat the vapour as an ideal gas.
L4|hard.solution:
## Part (a): Verify equilibrium at $T_1 = 194.65\,\text{K}$, $P_1 = 1\,\text{atm}$

At equilibrium between two phases, the molar Gibbs energy (chemical potential) of each phase must be equal, so $\Delta G_{\text{sub}} = 0$.

Compute directly:
$$\Delta G_{\text{sub}} = \Delta H_{\text{sub}} - T_1 \Delta S_{\text{sub}}$$
$$= 25{,}200 - (194.65)(129.4)$$
$$= 25{,}200 - 25{,}187.5$$
$$\approx +12.5\,\text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 0\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$

The small residual (~13 J mol⁻¹, less than 0.05% of $\Delta H$) is due to rounding in the given data. Within the precision of the supplied values, $\Delta G_{\text{sub}} \approx 0$, confirming that solid and gaseous CO₂ are in thermodynamic equilibrium at $194.65\,\text{K}$ and $1\,\text{atm}$. $\checkmark$

---

## Part (b): Vapour pressure at $T_2 = 170\,\text{K}$ via Clausius–Clapeyron

**Step 1 — State the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.**

For the solid–vapour boundary (sublimation), the Clausius–Clapeyron equation is:
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{sub}}}{RT^2}$$

Integrating from $(T_1, P_1)$ to $(T_2, P_2)$ with $\Delta H_{\text{sub}}$ constant:
$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_{\text{sub}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

**Step 2 — Substitute values.**

$$\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{170} - \frac{1}{194.65} = 5.882 \times 10^{-3} - 5.138 \times 10^{-3} = 7.44 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{25{,}200}{8.314} \times 7.44 \times 10^{-4}$$
$$= -3030.3 \times 7.44 \times 10^{-4}$$
$$= -2.255$$

**Step 3 — Solve for $P_2$.**

$$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = e^{-2.255} = 0.1047$$

$$\boxed{P_2 = 0.1047 \times 1.013 \times 10^5 = 1.060 \times 10^4\,\text{Pa} \approx 0.105\,\text{atm}}$$

Physical sense check: at lower temperature the vapour pressure of the solid is lower (fewer molecules have enough energy to escape the surface). A drop from 1 atm at 194.65 K to ~0.105 atm at 170 K is a factor of ~10 reduction over a 25 K decrease — steep, consistent with the relatively large $\Delta H_{\text{sub}}$.

---

## Part (c): Change in molar entropy of the gas phase due to pressure change, using a Maxwell relation

**Step 1 — Identify the relevant Maxwell relation.**

From the Gibbs free energy differential $\mathrm{d}G = -S\,\mathrm{d}T + V\,\mathrm{d}P$, the Maxwell relation is:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$$

This connects an entropy derivative (hard to measure directly) to a volume derivative (straightforward).

**Step 2 — Apply the ideal-gas simplification.**

For an ideal gas (per mole): $P\underline{V} = RT$, so $\underline{V} = RT/P$.
$$\left(\frac{\partial \underline{V}}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{R}{P}$$

Substituting into the Maxwell relation:
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\frac{R}{P}$$

**Step 3 — Integrate at constant temperature from $P_{\text{initial}}$ to $P_{\text{final}}$.**

The gas (vapour) is in equilibrium with solid CO₂ throughout. At $T_2 = 170\,\text{K}$, the equilibrium vapour pressure is $P_{\text{initial}} = P_2 = 1.060 \times 10^4\,\text{Pa}$ (from part b). When the container is heated to $T_1 = 194.65\,\text{K}$, the equilibrium vapour pressure rises back to $P_{\text{final}} = P_1 = 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}$.

However, part (c) asks specifically for the entropy change of the gas due to the **pressure change at constant temperature** (isothermal step only). We integrate:
$$\Delta S_{\text{gas, pressure}} = \int_{P_{\text{initial}}}^{P_{\text{final}}} \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T \mathrm{d}P = -R\int_{P_2}^{P_1} \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{P} = -R\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2}$$

**Step 4 — Substitute values.**

$$\frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{1.013 \times 10^5}{1.060 \times 10^4} = 9.557$$

$$\Delta S_{\text{gas, pressure}} = -R\ln(9.557) = -8.314 \times \ln(9.557)$$
$$= -8.314 \times 2.257$$
$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\text{gas, pressure}} \approx -18.77\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

**Interpretation:** When the pressure on the ideal gas phase is increased isothermally (as the vapour pressure rises from $P_2$ to $P_1$), the molar entropy of the vapour **decreases** by about $18.8\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. This makes physical sense: compressing a gas into a smaller effective volume reduces the number of accessible microstates, lowering entropy. The negative result is a direct consequence of the Maxwell relation and is consistent with $\Delta S = -R\ln(P_2/P_1)$ from L3.
L4|hard.final_answer: (a) $\Delta G_{\text{sub}} \approx 0\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$ — confirms equilibrium at $194.65\,\text{K}$, $1\,\text{atm}$. (b) $P_2 \approx 1.06 \times 10^4\,\text{Pa} \approx 0.105\,\text{atm}$ at $170\,\text{K}$. (c) $\Delta S_{\text{gas, pressure}} \approx -18.8\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
common_mistakes: Applying the full Clapeyron equation $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T = \Delta H/(T\Delta V)$ instead of the Clausius–Clapeyron approximation for the solid–vapour boundary. The Clausius–Clapeyron form assumes $\Delta V \approx V_{\text{gas}} = RT/P$, discarding the molar volume of the solid. Students sometimes include $\underline{V}_{\text{solid}}$ in $\Delta V$, which is unnecessary here since $\underline{V}_{\text{solid}} \ll \underline{V}_{\text{gas}}$ (the gas molar volume at 1 atm and 195 K is ~1600 cm³/mol versus 28 cm³/mol for the solid).

In part (c), confusing the total entropy change of the vapour (which would include the temperature contribution $\int C_P/T\,\mathrm{d}T$) with the entropy change due to pressure alone. The problem explicitly asks for the effect of the pressure change at constant temperature, which is the Maxwell-relation integral $-R\ln(P_1/P_2)$. Mixing in the thermal contribution doubles-counts the heating.

Inverting the ratio inside the logarithm in the Clausius–Clapeyron equation. Students sometimes write $\ln(P_1/P_2)$ on the left and $(1/T_1 - 1/T_2)$ on the right, getting the sign wrong. Always check: going to lower temperature ($T_2 < T_1$) must give lower vapour pressure ($P_2 < P_1$), so $\ln(P_2/P_1) < 0$ and the bracket $(1/T_2 - 1/T_1) > 0$ — the minus sign in front makes the product negative, consistent.

L5|easy.title: Entropy of Mixing in an Ideal Cu-Ni Alloy
L5|easy.statement:
Copper (Cu) and nickel (Ni) form a completely miscible isomorphous solid solution at all compositions. Consider 1 mole of a Cu-Ni alloy containing 40 at% Ni (i.e. $X_{\mathrm{Ni}} = 0.40$, $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.60$).

Assuming ideal solution behaviour:

**(a)** Calculate the molar entropy of mixing, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$, in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

**(b)** State whether $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is positive or negative, and explain in one sentence why this is always the case for an ideal solution at any composition between 0 and 1.

**Given:** Gas constant $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
L5|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the relevant equation

For an ideal binary solution the molar entropy of mixing is:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -R\left(X_{\mathrm{Cu}}\ln X_{\mathrm{Cu}} + X_{\mathrm{Ni}}\ln X_{\mathrm{Ni}}\right)$$

This comes directly from the ideal-solution Gibbs energy of mixing $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} = RT(X_A \ln X_A + X_B \ln X_B)$ differentiated with respect to $T$ at constant $P$ and composition:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -\left(\frac{\partial \Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}}}{\partial T}\right)_{P,X} = -R\sum_i X_i \ln X_i$$

## Step 2 — Substitute the mole fractions

With $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.60$ and $X_{\mathrm{Ni}} = 0.40$:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -8.314\left(0.60\ln 0.60 + 0.40\ln 0.40\right)$$

Evaluate each logarithm:

$$\ln 0.60 = -0.5108, \qquad \ln 0.40 = -0.9163$$

Substitute:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -8.314\left[(0.60)(-0.5108) + (0.40)(-0.9163)\right]$$

$$= -8.314\left[-0.3065 - 0.3665\right]$$

$$= -8.314\times(-0.6730)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} \approx +5.60 \;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}}$$

## Step 3 — Sign and physical interpretation

$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} > 0$ because for any $0 < X_i < 1$, $\ln X_i < 0$, so $\sum_i X_i \ln X_i < 0$ and the leading minus sign makes the whole expression positive. Physically, mixing increases the number of accessible microstates (more ways to arrange Cu and Ni atoms on the lattice than when they are segregated into pure blocks), so entropy always increases upon ideal mixing.

## Sanity check

The maximum entropy of mixing for a binary system occurs at $X_A = X_B = 0.50$:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\max} = R\ln 2 = 8.314 \times 0.6931 \approx 5.76\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$$

Our answer of $5.60$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ at $X_{\mathrm{Ni}} = 0.40$ is slightly less than the maximum (which occurs at $X = 0.50$) — consistent expectation. ✓
common_mistakes: **Dropping the minus sign.** Students often write $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = R\sum X_i \ln X_i$ without the leading negative, obtaining a negative entropy of mixing — which would violate the Second Law for spontaneous mixing. The correct formula is $-R\sum X_i \ln X_i$.

**Using weight percent instead of mole fractions.** The formula requires dimensionless mole fractions $X_i$. If a student mistakenly inserts weight fractions (e.g. wt% Cu / 100) instead of at% mole fractions, they get a slightly different (incorrect) number. Always confirm that $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} + X_{\mathrm{Ni}} = 1$ as a check.

**Assuming $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = 0$ because Cu-Ni is an ideal solution.** It is $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = 0$ for an ideal solution — not the entropy. The entropy of mixing is always non-zero (and positive) for any mixture; zero $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the defining property of an ideal solution, not zero $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$.

L5|easy.title: Entropy of Mixing in a Binary Gold–Silver Ideal Solution
L5|easy.statement:
Gold (Au) and silver (Ag) are known to form a nearly ideal substitutional solid solution at elevated temperatures, because both are FCC metals with very similar atomic radii and electronegativities. Consider preparing 1 mole of a homogeneous Au–Ag alloy containing $X_{\text{Au}} = 0.30$ (mole fraction of gold) at constant temperature and pressure.

(a) Calculate the molar entropy of mixing, $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$, when this ideal solution is formed from the pure components.

(b) State the molar enthalpy of mixing and the molar Gibbs free energy of mixing for this ideal solution at $T = 1000\,\text{K}$, explaining your reasoning.

Useful constants: $R = 8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
L5|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the mole fractions

For a binary Au–Ag system, the two mole fractions must sum to unity:
$$X_{\text{Au}} = 0.30, \qquad X_{\text{Ag}} = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70$$

## Part (a) — Molar entropy of mixing

For an **ideal binary solution**, the molar entropy of mixing is:
$$\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = -R\left(X_{\text{Au}}\ln X_{\text{Au}} + X_{\text{Ag}}\ln X_{\text{Ag}}\right)$$

Substitute values:
$$\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = -8.314\left(0.30\ln 0.30 + 0.70\ln 0.70\right)$$

Evaluate the logarithms:
$$\ln 0.30 = -1.2040, \qquad \ln 0.70 = -0.3567$$

Calculate each term:
$$0.30 \times (-1.2040) = -0.3612$$
$$0.70 \times (-0.3567) = -0.2497$$

Sum inside the brackets:
$$-0.3612 + (-0.2497) = -0.6109$$

Apply the leading $-R$:
$$\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = -8.314 \times (-0.6109) = +5.08\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = +5.08\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

The positive sign is expected: mixing always increases the number of accessible microstates (atoms can now be distributed across all lattice sites), so entropy increases.

## Part (b) — Enthalpy and Gibbs free energy of mixing

**Enthalpy of mixing:**

For an ideal solution, all A–A, B–B, and A–B pair bond energies are equivalent (the bond-energy parameter $\varepsilon = 0$). Therefore no energy is released or absorbed on mixing:
$$\boxed{\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = 0}$$

**Gibbs free energy of mixing at $T = 1000\,\text{K}$:**

Using $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = \Delta H_{\text{mix}} - T\,\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$:
$$\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = 0 - (1000\,\text{K})(5.08\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})$$
$$\boxed{\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = -5080\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = -5.08\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

Because $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} < 0$, the mixing is **spontaneous** at 1000 K — the ideal Au–Ag solid solution is thermodynamically stable relative to the separated pure components.
L5|easy.final_answer: (a) $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = +5.08\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$; (b) $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = 0$, $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = -5.08\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ at 1000 K
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in front of $R$ in the ideal-solution entropy formula, giving a negative $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$ — entropy of mixing for an ideal solution is always positive because $\ln X_i < 0$ for $0 < X_i < 1$ and the two negatives cancel.

Assuming $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} \neq 0$ because gold and silver are different elements. In an ideal solution by definition all bond energies are equivalent and $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = 0$ exactly; the non-zero mixing Gibbs energy is driven entirely by the entropy term $-T\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$.

Using $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = \Delta H_{\text{mix}} + T\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$ (wrong sign on the entropy term) instead of $\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = \Delta H_{\text{mix}} - T\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$, which would give a positive (non-spontaneous) result.

L5|easy.title: Activity Coefficient of Tin in a Lead-Tin Alloy
L5|easy.statement:
A lead-tin (Pb-Sn) solder alloy is prepared at 500 K containing 15 at% Sn. Experiments show that the equilibrium vapour pressure of Sn over this alloy is $P_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 4.20 \times 10^{-7}$ atm, while the vapour pressure of pure liquid tin at the same temperature is $P^*_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 2.10 \times 10^{-6}$ atm.

(a) Calculate the activity of tin in the alloy, $a_{\mathrm{Sn}}$.

(b) Calculate the activity coefficient of tin in the alloy, $\gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}}$.

(c) State whether this solution shows a positive or negative deviation from ideal (Raoult's Law) behaviour, and briefly explain what this implies about the Sn–Pb bond strength relative to like-like bonds.
L5|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Recall the relevant definitions

For a component $i$ in a liquid or solid solution, activity is defined via the ratio of its fugacity (approximated by its partial vapour pressure for an ideal vapour) to its standard-state fugacity (vapour pressure of the pure component in the same physical state):

$$a_i = \frac{f_i}{f_i^\circ} \approx \frac{P_i}{P_i^*}$$

The activity coefficient $\gamma_i$ relates activity to mole fraction through:

$$a_i = \gamma_i X_i$$

For an ideal solution obeying Raoult's Law, $\gamma_i = 1$ and $a_i = X_i$.

---

## Part (a) — Activity of Sn

Substitute the given vapour pressures directly:

$$a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{Sn}}}{P^*_{\mathrm{Sn}}} = \frac{4.20 \times 10^{-7}\;\mathrm{atm}}{2.10 \times 10^{-6}\;\mathrm{atm}}$$

$$\boxed{a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.200}$$

---

## Part (b) — Activity coefficient of Sn

The mole fraction of Sn is given as $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.15$ (15 at%).

Using $a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}} X_{\mathrm{Sn}}$, solve for $\gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}}$:

$$\gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}} = \frac{a_{\mathrm{Sn}}}{X_{\mathrm{Sn}}} = \frac{0.200}{0.15}$$

$$\boxed{\gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 1.33}$$

---

## Part (c) — Sign of deviation and physical interpretation

Since $\gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}} > 1$, the alloy shows a **positive deviation** from Raoult's Law. The activity of Sn is higher than its mole fraction would predict for an ideal solution.

Physically, a positive deviation ($\gamma > 1$) means tin atoms have a higher escaping tendency in the alloy than in a hypothetical ideal mixture. This implies that **Sn–Pb bonds are weaker than the average of Sn–Sn and Pb–Pb like-like bonds** (i.e. the bond-energy parameter $\varepsilon = E_{\mathrm{SnPb}} - \tfrac{1}{2}(E_{\mathrm{SnSn}} + E_{\mathrm{PbPb}}) > 0$). Tin is less comfortable surrounded by lead neighbours than by tin neighbours, so it has a higher tendency to escape into the vapour phase.

**Sanity check:** For an ideal Raoult's Law solution, $a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = X_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.15$. We got $a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.20 > 0.15$, confirming positive deviation. ✓
L5|easy.final_answer: (a) $a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.200$; (b) $\gamma_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 1.33$; (c) Positive deviation — Sn–Pb bonds are weaker than the average of like-like bonds ($\varepsilon > 0$).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert at% directly to mole fraction: since the problem already states '15 at% Sn', the mole fraction is directly $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.15$. Students sometimes attempt an unnecessary wt%-to-mol% conversion.

Inverting the activity ratio as $P^*_{\mathrm{Sn}} / P_{\mathrm{Sn}}$ instead of $P_{\mathrm{Sn}} / P^*_{\mathrm{Sn}}$, giving $a_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 5.0$ (greater than 1, which is physically impossible for a condensed-phase component relative to its pure-liquid standard state at the same temperature).

Confusing the sign of deviation: students may see $\gamma > 1$ and mistakenly associate it with 'more stable' or 'negative deviation'. Positive deviation ($\gamma > 1$, activity above ideal) means like-like bonds are preferred and the solution is energetically less stable than an ideal mixture, not more.

L5|easy.title: Entropy of Mixing in a Binary Ideal Alloy
L5|easy.statement:
A materials engineer prepares a binary ideal solid solution by mixing pure nickel (Ni) and pure copper (Cu) at 1100 K. The alloy contains 65 at% Ni and 35 at% Cu. Assume the solution behaves ideally.

Calculate the molar entropy of mixing, $\Delta S_\text{mix}$, for this alloy.

Given: $R = 8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
L5|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the ideal-solution formula for $\Delta S_\text{mix}$

For an ideal binary solution, the molar entropy of mixing is:
$$\Delta S_\text{mix} = -R\left(X_\text{Ni}\ln X_\text{Ni} + X_\text{Cu}\ln X_\text{Cu}\right)$$

This follows from differentiating $\Delta G_\text{mix} = RT(X_A \ln X_A + X_B \ln X_B)$ with respect to temperature at constant pressure and composition:
$$\Delta S_\text{mix} = -\left(\frac{\partial \Delta G_\text{mix}}{\partial T}\right)_{P,X} = -R\sum_i X_i \ln X_i$$

## Step 2 — Identify mole fractions

The alloy is given in at% (atomic percent), which is equivalent to mole fraction for an elemental binary:
$$X_\text{Ni} = 0.65, \qquad X_\text{Cu} = 0.35$$

## Step 3 — Compute the logarithmic terms

$$\ln X_\text{Ni} = \ln(0.65) = -0.4308$$
$$\ln X_\text{Cu} = \ln(0.35) = -1.0498$$

## Step 4 — Evaluate $\Delta S_\text{mix}$

$$\Delta S_\text{mix} = -R\left[(0.65)(-0.4308) + (0.35)(-1.0498)\right]$$
$$= -8.314 \times \left[-0.2800 - 0.3674\right]$$
$$= -8.314 \times (-0.6474)$$
$$\boxed{\Delta S_\text{mix} \approx +5.38\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 5 — Sanity check

The answer is positive, as expected — mixing always increases entropy for an ideal solution because the number of accessible microstates increases. The maximum $\Delta S_\text{mix}$ for a binary occurs at $X = 0.5$ and equals $R\ln 2 \approx 5.76\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Our value (5.38) is slightly below this maximum, consistent with a composition (65/35) that is moderately close to but not exactly 50/50. The temperature of 1100 K does not enter the entropy-of-mixing formula — it is included in $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ but not $\Delta S_\text{mix}$ for an ideal solution.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in front of $R$. Since $0 < X_i < 1$, all $\ln X_i < 0$, so the double negative gives a positive $\Delta S_\text{mix}$. Students who drop the leading minus sign report a negative entropy of mixing, which would violate the Second Law for an ideal solution.

Using weight percent directly as mole fractions. The problem states at% (atomic percent), which equals mole fraction for elemental components. If the composition were given in wt%, conversion to mole fractions using molar masses would be required first.

Multiplying the result by temperature $T$ to get $\Delta G_\text{mix}$ and reporting that as the entropy. $\Delta S_\text{mix} = -R\sum X_i \ln X_i$ does not involve $T$; it is temperature-independent for an ideal solution. The temperature 1100 K appears in $\Delta G_\text{mix} = RT\sum X_i \ln X_i$, not in the entropy itself.

L5|easy.title: Entropy of Mixing in a Binary Brass Alloy
L5|easy.statement:
A binary alloy is formed by mixing pure copper (Cu) and pure zinc (Zn) to produce single-phase brass containing $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.30$ (mole fraction of Zn), with $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.70$. Treating the solution as ideal, calculate the molar entropy of mixing $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ (in J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). Also state whether this value confirms that mixing is spontaneous from an entropic standpoint, and identify the composition at which $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$ would be maximised.

Given: $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
L5|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Identify the relevant equation

For an ideal binary solution, the molar entropy of mixing is

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -R\left(X_A \ln X_A + X_B \ln X_B\right)$$

where $X_A$ and $X_B$ are the mole fractions of the two components. Here $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.70$ and $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = 0.30$.

## Step 2 — Compute the logarithmic terms

$$\ln(0.70) = -0.3567, \qquad \ln(0.30) = -1.2040$$

## Step 3 — Substitute into the formula

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} = -8.314\,\bigl[(0.70)(−0.3567) + (0.30)(−1.2040)\bigr]$$

$$= -8.314\,\bigl[-0.2497 - 0.3612\bigr]$$

$$= -8.314 \times (-0.6109)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} \approx +5.08 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

## Step 4 — Interpret the sign

Since $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} > 0$, mixing **increases** entropy, confirming that the entropic driving force always favours mixing in an ideal solution. For an ideal solution $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}} = 0$, so $\Delta G_{\mathrm{mix}} = -T\,\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}} < 0$ at any positive temperature — mixing is spontaneous.

## Step 5 — Identify the composition of maximum $\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}$

The function $-R(X\ln X + (1-X)\ln(1-X))$ is maximised when $X_{\mathrm{Zn}} = X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.50$ (the equimolar composition). At that point:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\max} = -R(0.5\ln 0.5 + 0.5\ln 0.5) = R\ln 2 \approx 5.76 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$
